text.p: Liechtenstein faces its first political shakeup in over half a century as its coalition government seems set to split next week, government officials said on Friday.

The tiny Alpine principality with a population of 31,000 and covering just 160 square km (62 square miles) is noted more in neighbouring Switzerland and Austria as an off-shore banking centre and for its smoked Malbuner ham than for its politics.

It has been governed by the same partnership of the Fatherland Union (VU) and Progressive Citizens Party Liechtenstein (FBPL) since 1938, when the parties joined to show solidarity against Nazi Germany.
Political observers say there has been no discernible difference between the two parties except for the personalities of their leaders.

But the FBPL has been losing votes since 1978. The balance was finally tipped in general elections on February 2, when the pro-ecology Free List party, which has been represented in parliament with one seat since 1993, gained a second seat at the expense of the FBPL.
The move left the FBPL with only 10 seats, down from 11.
The VU holds the remaining 13 seats.
The FBPL will decide at a party meeting on Monday whether to approve its leadership's proposal to break the coalition, said its president, Norbert Seeger.
He believes the move to split would be positive for the country and also for the FBPL, which hopes to raise its profile by forming a real opposition party.

"When you are in a coalition government, this also binds parliament to certain decisions. We believe through this move, if it passes, the parliament will gain a stronger position, and will also be facing stronger challenges," Seeger said by telephone from Vaduz.
Liechtenstein's central government consists of a prime minister and four government councillors.
It forms a link between the parliament and the ruling hereditary prince, 52-year-old Prince Hans Adam of Liechtenstein, who is head of state.
Prince Philipp, Hans Adam's brother, said the latest changes may turn out to be good for the country.

"It is much better to have somebody who is responsible, and somebody who is on the other side, and not to mix the two things," he told Reuters at a presentation of LGT Group, the Vaduz-based bank, emphasising he was giving a private opinion.
"For the first time the opposition is really an opposition, and we truly have to work out how to deal with each other after more than 50 years of coalition."
United as a principality since 1719, Liechtenstein has had a constitutional government since 1862.
